st.headline: SK Hynix puts US IPO of chip unit Solidigm on hold after Seoul authorities raise concerns
st.teaser: The South Korean chip giant said it plans to continue to explore ways to fund Solidigm’s expansion.
fullText: SEOUL – SK Hynix on Oct 23 put on hold a planned US listing for its Solidigm chip unit due to market volatility – a move which also comes after the South Korean authorities raised concerns that the deal could undermine shareholder interests.

A listing of Solidigm, a former Intel business that specialises in NAND flash memory and solid-state drives, had been under consideration to help fund a new US factory and meet surging demand for chips in artificial intelligence data centres.
It could also have funded share cancellations and buybacks, SK Hynix said in a statement.
People familiar with the now-suspended initial public offering plans had said that the share sale could have raised US$15 billion (S$19.1 billion) valued the unit at US$150 billion.

The South Korean chip giant, which became dual-listed with a debut on the Nasdaq in July, said it plans to continue to explore ways to fund Solidigm’s expansion and enhance shareholder value, including reviewing the timing, scale and financing of future investments.
“This decision does not reflect any change in Solidigm’s growth prospects or investment needs,” it said.

It was not immediately clear how the decision would be received by the Trump administration, which has put pressure on foreign chipmakers to build new facilities in the US and which has been holding discussions with SK Hynix.

According to sources familiar with the matter, SK Hynix has sought to use the prospect of a potential factory in the US as a bargaining chip, linking it to hoped-for approval from Washington that would allow US chipmaking equipment to be exported to China to increase production there.

The South Korean authorities have said they are discussing semiconductor investments in the US with Washington as part of broader bilateral talks, but they are not part of negotiations about a US$350 billion investment commitment South Korea made to the US in 2025 in exchange for lower US tariffs.

Across the globe, sentiment towards AI and chip-related stocks has retreated sharply as investors increasingly fret over whether rising interest rates will mean that companies involved in building out the AI supply chain will make sufficient earnings to repay their debts.
At the same time, in South Korea, concerns also have mounted that a listing of Solidigm in the US would dilute the interests of SK Hynix shareholders.

Financial Supervisory Service governor Lee Chan-jin told a parliamentary hearing this week that regulators were examining whether Solidigm’s potential US IPO would require a review under the country’s dual-listing restrictions, which were tightened in July to strengthen shareholder protections.

In addition to broad concerns about the AI sector, worries that a Solidigm IPO could dilute SK Hynix shareholders’ interests have weighed on the chipmaker’s shares, which have tumbled 31% since news of the potential listing emerged in late September.
That compares with a 20% decline in the benchmark KOSPI index over the same period.
The Korea Corporate Governance Forum, an independent body, welcomed SK Hynix’s decision.

Instead of a US listing for Solidigm, the chipmaker, which has made massive earnings gains on the AI boom, could instead inject capital through its AI Company entity, even if Solidigm requires tens of trillions of won in capital expenditure, it said.
Citing average estimates from South Korean brokerages, it said SK Hynix’s cash holdings were projected to reach 456 trillion won (S$439.9 billion) by the end of 2027.
SK Hynix shares were up 1.4% in afternoon trade, outperforming a 1.4% decline in the KOSPI. REUTERS

cna.headline: Singapore’s core inflation eases to 2% in September on lower services, retail prices
cna.teaser: A "sharp and sustained surge" in global energy or food prices could lift Singapore’s import costs by more than projected, say MAS and METI.
fullText: SINGAPORE: Singapore’s core inflation eased to 2 per cent year-on-year in September, down from 2.2 per cent in August, according to official figures released on Friday (Oct 23).

This was because of lower inflation in services, retail and other goods and private transport, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry (METI) said in a joint media release.
Core prices, which exclude accommodation and private transport, rose by 0.1 per cent month-on-month in September.

Overall inflation, as measured by the Consumer Price Index-All Items, fell to 2.2 per cent year-on-year in September from 2.3 per cent in August, due to lower core inflation and private transport inflation.

Official data released on Friday showed that services inflation eased to 1.7 per cent in September from 2 per cent in August due to a smaller increase in point-to-point transport service costs and a larger decline in telecommunication service prices.
Retail and other goods inflation also moderated to 1.2 per cent in September from 1.8 per cent in August as furniture prices declined and clothing prices rose at a slower pace.
Private transport inflation also fell to 7.1 per cent in September from 7.5 per cent in August due to a more gradual increase in car prices.
Electricity and gas inflation was unchanged at 8.7 per cent as prices rose at a similar pace in both September and August.

MAS and METI noted that the regulated electricity tariff for each quarter is set based largely on the average natural gas prices in the first two and a half months of the preceding quarter, among other factors.

“The increase in the regulated electricity tariff in the third quarter of 2026 is thus the result of the spike in global energy prices over the period of April to mid-June 2026,” the authorities said.
Accommodation inflation edged up to 0.9 per cent in September from 0.8 per cent in August, with housing rents increasing at a faster pace.
Food inflation also rose to 2.4 per cent in September from 2.3 per cent in August due to higher inflation in both non-cooked food and food services.
The authorities said that imported cost pressures are expected to remain firm for Singapore in the near term.
“Energy commodity prices have risen anew and are projected to remain high in the near term,” said MAS and METI.
“Global and regional food prices are also expected to pick up as costlier inputs and adverse weather patterns affect food production.”
But imported inflation should ease over 2027 as the effects of temporary supply disruptions fade, the authorities added.
On the domestic front, price pressures are likely to stay subdued, with unit labour costs in the services sector expected to remain contained amid continued productivity gains, MAS and METI said.
Enhanced government subsidies, such as for healthcare and education, will also dampen services inflation, the authorities added.
Taking into account these factors, core inflation and overall inflation are expected to remain slightly elevated in the immediate quarters ahead before easing more discernibly from mid-2027.
Core inflation is expected to average 1.5 per cent to 2 per cent in 2026, in line with MAS' full-year forecast range . It is also expected to average 1.5 per cent to 2.5 per cent in 2027.
Overall inflation is expected at around 2 per cent in 2026 and 1.5 per cent to 2.5 per cent in 2027.
“The risks to inflation remain tilted to the upside. A sharp and sustained surge in global energy or food prices could lift Singapore’s import costs by more than projected,” MAS and METI said.
Domestic inflation could also stay elevated if spillovers from the artificial intelligence-related boom broaden and unit labour costs rise more rapidly, the authorities added.
“However, higher-than-expected global interest rates or a pullback in AI-related investment could exert a drag on growth, and thus, inflation,” MAS and METI said.
“Energy production and shipments from the Middle East could also recover more quickly than projected, resulting in a greater decline in energy prices.”

mom.headline: Additional Guidance for Employers on Use of 1-Hour PM2.5 Readings to Protect Outdoor Workers During Haze
mom.teaser: 1 The Ministry of Manpower (MOM) has issued new guidance on how employers should adjust outdoor work based on the 1-hour PM2.5 readings. This complements the existing guidance based on the PSI forecast, and helps employers respond within the day as air quality changes.

listening.title: Singapore Expands Solar Adoption Across HDB Estates
listening.transcript: Singapore is ramping up its clean energy efforts by installing solar panels across thousands of public housing blocks. Officials say the initiative aims to generate enough electricity to power common services like lifts and corridor lighting. Economists note that while initial capital costs are substantial, the long-term environmental and financial returns will be immense. Local residents have welcomed the move, seeing it as a tangible step toward urban sustainability.

economistArticle.title: Rethinking the China Shock: Was Trade Really to Blame?
paras: Two decades ago, China's accession to the World Trade Organisation triggered a monumental shift in global commerce. A landmark body of academic research, coined the 'China shock' literature, argued that rapid Chinese import penetration crippled manufacturing communities in Western nations, causing persistent job losses that standard economic models had failed to anticipate.

However, fresh empirical research is challenging this conventional wisdom, sparking an almighty fight among economists. New studies suggest that earlier models overestimated the negative impact by focusing narrowly on local labour markets while ignoring the broader compensatory mechanisms within regional supply chains.

Re-evaluations reveal that lower import prices significantly reduced production costs for downstream domestic firms, enabling them to expand and generate secondary employment. Furthermore, cheap consumer goods bolstered real incomes, indirectly stimulating demand across service sectors that were previously omitted from the analytical scope.

This academic squabble is far from an esoteric dispute; it carries profound geopolitical ramifications. If trade integration was not the primary driver of industrial decline, then the aggressive tariffs and protectionist policies championed by contemporary politicians may be targeting the wrong culprit altogether.

Ultimately, defusing the 'China shock' narrative requires recognizing that structural technological shifts played a far more decisive role in eroding factory jobs. By misattributing technological disruption to global trade, policymakers risk enacting remedies that worsen economic welfare rather than safeguarding it.
economistArticle.cn:
二十年前，中国加入世界贸易组织引发了全球贸易的巨变。被称为“中国冲击”文献的里程碑式学术研究指出，中国进口商品的快速渗透压垮了西方国家的制造业社区，导致了标准经济模型未能预测到的持久失业。
然而，最新的实证研究正在挑战这一传统观点，并在经济学界引发了一场激烈的争论。新研究表明，早期模型过于专注于局部劳动力市场，却忽视了区域供应链内更广泛的补偿机制，从而高估了其负面影响。
重新评估表明，较低的进口价格显著降低了下游本土企业的生产成本，使其能够扩张并创造二次就业机会。此外，廉价的消费品拉动了实际收入，间接刺激了此前被排除在分析范围之外的服务业需求。
这场学术争吵绝非离奇古怪的偏僻争端，它具有深刻的地缘政治影响。如果贸易一体化并非工业衰退的主要推手，那么当代政治家所倡导的激进关税和保护主义政策，可能完全针对错了罪魁祸首。
归根结底，拆解“中国冲击”这一叙事需要认识到，结构性技术变革在削弱工厂岗位方面发挥了远为决定性的作用。通过将技术颠覆错怪给全球贸易，政策制定者冒着制定出恶化经济福利而非保障福利的政策风险。

gems.why: Uses a contrastive participial clause ('By misattributing...') to clearly highlight the cause-and-effect relationship between flawed analysis and bad policy. 通过使用对比分词状语从句（“通过将...错怪给...”），清晰指出了错误分析与糟糕政策之间的因果关系。
